title: Must the arcs above and below X Y have the same radius?
description: A question from the book asks whether the arcs above the segment and the arcs below it need one radius. A construction with two different radii is drawn, and two congruent triangle pairs show why the line still cuts X Y in half at a right angle.
teaching_notes: One idea: each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so each lies on the perpendicular bisector, and two points fix the line. Watch for students who think all four arcs must share one radius.

video_script.why: The child has followed the construction with one radius throughout and has not yet asked whether the radius above may differ from the radius below.
video_script.substitution: The construction is done in the same way as the example in the book, with a different radius for the lower pair of arcs, and then the triangles explain why it still works.
video_script.anchor: Is it necessary to have the same radius for the arcs above and below X Y?
video_script.payoff_line: No, the two radii need not be equal

final_answer.value: No. The radius above may differ from the radius below; A and B are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and two points fix the line
final_answer.spoken: no, the two radii need not be equal, because each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, and two points fix the line

never_show: the answer no before the answer line
maths_rules: Radius r from X and from Y above XY, r more than half of XY, meets at A: AX = AY = r.
A different radius s from X and from Y below XY, s more than half of XY, meets at B: BX = BY = s.
Triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so angle XAO = angle YAO where AB meets XY at O.
Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS (AX = AY, equal angles at A, AO common), so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
A and B are each equally far from X and Y, and two points fix one line, so line AB is the perpendicular bisector.
video_script.design: One idea: the lower arcs may have a different radius from the upper arcs, because each meeting point is equally far from X and Y on its own. The construction of the book's example is repeated, and the same two congruences explain it.
